title: Beslan school siege
wiki_lead:
The Beslan school siege, also referred to as the Beslan terror attack, the Beslan tragedy, or the Beslan massacre, was an Islamist terrorist attack that occurred from 1 September 2004 to 3 September 2004 in Beslan, North Ossetia, Russia. It lasted three days, and involved the imprisonment of more than 1,100 people as hostages, including 777 children. The hostages, primarily children, their parents, and school staff were held by terrorists in a building rigged with explosives under severe conditions; the terrorists did not provide them with food or water and denied them other basic necessities. The siege ended with the deaths of 334 people, 186 of them children, as well as 31 of the attackers. It is considered the deadliest school shooting in history. 
The crisis began when a group of armed terrorists occupied School Number One (SNO) in the town of Beslan, North Ossetia (a republic in the North Caucasus region of Russia), on 1 September 2004. The hostage-takers were members of the Riyad-us Saliheen, sent by the Chechen warlord Shamil Basayev, who demanded Russia withdraw from and recognize the independence of Chechnya. On the third day of the standoff, Russian security forces stormed the building.
Official accounts of the attack's motive broadly agree that it was executed to destabilize the North Caucasus and was Islamist in nature. Right after the conclusion of the attack, in a televised address, Vladimir Putin outlined the attack as a "direct intervention of international terror", and the federal parliamentary commission attributed it to Chechen separatists ordered by Shamil Basayev whose Riyad-us Saliheen Brigade claimed responsibility for the attack. Widespread evidence from victim testimonies identify the terrorists as an Islamist group, as terrorists shouted Allahu Akbar throughout the attacks and during hostage negotiation, Basayev ended his ransom note to Putin with the same words
The event had security and political repercussions in Russia, leading to a series of federal government reforms consolidating power in the Kremlin and strengthening the powers of the President of Russia. Criticisms of the Russian government's management of the crisis have persisted, including allegations of disinformation and censorship in news media as well as questions about journalistic freedom, negotiations with the terrorists, allocation of responsibility for the eventual outcome and the use of excessive force.

Background

School No. 1 was one of seven schools in Beslan, a town of about 35,000 people in the Republic of North Ossetia–Alania in Russia's Caucasus. The school, located next to the district police station, housed approximately 60 teachers and more than 800 students. Its gymnasium, where most of the hostages were held for 52 hours, was a recent addition, measuring 10 metres (33 ft) wide and 25 metres (82 ft) long. grok_lead: The Beslan school siege was a terrorist hostage crisis from September 1 to 3, 2004, in which 32 heavily armed militantsâpredominantly Chechen and Ingush Islamists affiliated with the Riyad-us Saliheen Martyrs' Brigadeâstormed School Number One in Beslan, North Ossetia-Alania, Russia, during the first day of classes, capturing approximately 1,200 hostages, the majority of whom were children and accompanying adults. The attackers, who arrived in a hijacked truck and truck bomb, herded victims into the gymnasium, wired the building with improvised explosive devices, and executed several hostages early on while issuing demands for Russian withdrawal from Chechnya and the release of militants held in other incidents. Masterminded and publicly claimed by Chechen jihadist commander Shamil Basayev, the operation exemplified the escalating tactics of Islamist insurgents in the Second Chechen War, blending separatist grievances with calls for an Islamic emirate in the North Caucasus. Negotiations yielded limited releases of infants and some mothers but stalled amid the militants' intransigence and conflicting reports on hostage numbers, which Russian authorities initially underestimated at around 350 despite evidence of far more. On the third day, multiple explosionsâtriggered by the terrorists' bombs in the overcrowded gymâcaused structural collapse and ignited fires, killing scores instantly and prompting a disorganized assault by Russian special forces using infantry, armored vehicles, and flame-throwers to suppress the remaining fighters. The operation concluded with the elimination of 31 attackers, but not before over 330 hostages perished, including 186 children, marking it as the deadliest terrorist incident in Russia's post-Soviet history and exposing operational lapses in intelligence, crisis management, and force application, as later critiqued by the European Court of Human Rights for inadequate prevention and planning despite the militants' primary culpability in initiating and detonating the explosives. The siege's aftermath fueled debates over counterterrorism efficacy, with Basayev's subsequent killing in 2006 by Russian forces underscoring the jihadist network's persistence, while local Ossetian communities grappled with profound trauma, evidenced by high rates of psychological distress among survivors and demands for accountability that highlighted tensions between empirical accountability and state narratives.
